summary: Boston Harbor light lit 1890 on an iron caisson; abandoned 1972; torn down 1982; a skeletal tower on a pile platform since 2015; closed, best seen from the water.

light.original_order: fourth (archive) or fifth (LighthouseFriends quoting 1890 Board records)
light.original_characteristic: fixed white varied by a red flash every 28 seconds (LighthouseFriends quoting 1890 Board records)

structures.note: Iron tower 37 feet from base to focal plane, on a cylinder iron caisson 33 feet in diameter; demolished 1982 (LighthouseFriends; archive)
White fiberglass tower on the old base, 1982 (LighthouseFriends; the archive dates it 1983); brown fiberglass 1984; removed 2015 (LighthouseFriends)
Square skeletal tower on a nearby pile-supported platform (LighthouseFriends; archive: steel skeletal tower installed 2015)

access.note: The Coast Guard owns the lighthouse and the tower is closed. Best seen from the water; the offshore light can be seen from the island's public walkway (LighthouseFriends).

events.note: Boston Marine Society petitions Congress for a stone beacon on Deer Island's southern point (granite pyramid, painted red)
Congress appropriates $35,000 (4 August 1886); a further $6,000 on 2 October 1888
Cylinder iron caisson and iron tower finished 31 December 1889 (LighthouseFriends, quoting 1890 Board records)
Light established at Deer Island (archive: established 1890)
Original optic: fourth order per the archive; fifth order per the 1890 Board records as quoted by LighthouseFriends
Window in the pier stove in by the sea; replaced by a 15-inch ship's side light
Steamer John Endicott sinks a sloop yacht; the keeper rescues two in the station dory (LighthouseFriends)
Two black can buoys marking a channel through mine fields between Deer Island and Long Island Head lights discontinued 6 August 1898 (Board report, fiscal 1899)
November 1898 Portland Gale: windows smashed, cistern spoiled, dory and landing ladder swept about (LighthouseFriends)
Assistant Keeper Elno C. Mott rescues two men from a burning motor boat (night of 11 July 1914)
Mott brings in the disabled power boat Alice; eleven men given food and lodging (11 September 1915)
Keepers McCabe and Mott tow the power boat Madeline to a safe anchorage (22 September 1915)
Keeper Joseph B. McCabe drowned on the bar on Saturday night, 19 February 1916, newspapers say while running to light the lamp; LighthouseFriends gives a different errand (see notes)
Keeper Mott brings a disabled motor boat with five people to a safe anchorage (23 September 1917)
Illuminant changed from oil to electric incandescent
27 December 1930 storm; Keeper Merrill King stuffs cotton into cracks in the walls (LighthouseFriends)
Winter ice cracks the cast-iron caisson; encircled with steel sheet piling and riprap (LighthouseFriends)
Light abandoned 19 February 1972 after a February storm; crew taken off by the cutter Pendant (LighthouseFriends)
Original 1890 tower demolished; demolition began 14 June 1982 and was finished three weeks later
White fiberglass tower erected on the old base ($100,000)
Brown fiberglass tower takes the place of the white one
Fiberglass tower removed (November 2015); square skeletal tower on a nearby pile-supported platform

corrections.why: LighthouseFriends says the site title came from the City of Boston, and Boston lies in Suffolk County. The record's Essex is not supported by any source read.
The archive gives the tower material as CAST IRON, on a pier or caisson foundation; LighthouseFriends describes a cylinder iron caisson with an iron tower.

corrections.proposed: unstaffed, as of 1972 (keepers abandoned the light on 19 February 1972)
corrections.why: The archive's keeper lines run to 1972, and LighthouseFriends says the light was abandoned in February 1972. Nothing read supports an automation date of 1960.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 2015 date is the current skeletal tower, and 1890 is the original cast-iron tower. Both belong to the station; the story treats them as separate structures.
The archive says the 1890 tower does not exist, and OpenStreetMap maps a structure today. The 1890 tower was torn down in 1982; the 2015 skeletal tower is what the map shows.

notes_for_editor: 1) Lens order: the archive records a fourth-order optic installed 1890; LighthouseFriends quotes the 1890 Board records as describing a fifth-order light. Not resolved; the story states both. 2) Dates: LighthouseFriends dates completion to 31 December 1889; the archive and Rowlett's record give 1890 for the light. The story gives both. 3) Staffing: the record's automation date of 1960 (from Wikidata) is not supported by the archive, whose keeper lines run to 1972, or by LighthouseFriends, which says the light was abandoned on 19 February 1972. The correction proposes unstaffed as of 1972. 4) The record's county 'Essex' looks wrong: the site title came from the City of Boston (LighthouseFriends), and Boston lies in Suffolk County. Proposed as a correction. 5) Current tower date: LighthouseFriends and the archive give November 2015; Wikipedia (not cited) gives 2016. The story uses 2015. 6) Same name, different place: Deer Island Thoroughfare, Maine (a light on Mark Island, Penobscot Bay) appears in the same Board reports and in the 1918 to 1923 Bulletin index (Holt, Allen C.). None of those entries is used. 7) Roster: matched by name and position to the USLHS place 'Deer Island' (0.04 km); the archive prints the town as 'Bostob'. Roles: the roster tool normalised 'Principal Lighthouse Keeper' to 'head keeper'. Marticio's span is printed '-1972' with no start year; the JSON omits the unknown start. 8) McCabe, 19 February 1916: the Daily Kennebec Journal (21 February 1916) and the Manchester Journal (24 February 1916) report the drowning on the bar on Saturday night, the first while running to light the lamp and the second giving his age as 35. LighthouseFriends gives a different errand (help with wedding invitations), age 28, and a body never found. The story gives both accounts. The newspapers print the name Joseph R. McCabe; the archive and the Bulletins say Joseph B. McCabe, and the keeper is identified as the same man by the Board position and dates. The 1895 yacht rescue, the 1898 Portland Gale, the 1930 storm, the 1936 ice and the 1972 abandonment are LighthouseFriends accounts only. 9) The 1891 window and bell (scan p. 61), the 1898 buoys (scan p. 96) and the Bulletin rescues are read from OCR; the Bulletin 1915 Madeline passage was matched by its distinctive phrase, and the page images were not viewed. 10) Privacy: the keepers named are historical (1890 to 1972). Marticio is named only as LighthouseFriends prints his account, in his public role. The LighthouseFriends anecdotes about a keeper's cat and a Prohibition-era incident are left out. 11) LighthouseFriends is used for facts, and its quotations are limited to short phrases; the Board, Bulletin and Commissioner passages are short quotations from public-domain government reports. 12) Fact-check 2026-10-27: the archive's Disposition field dates the fiberglass tower that replaced the 1890 tower to 1983; LighthouseFriends dates it to 1982 (demolition June 1982). The story gives both. 13) The archive's Tower Shape for the 1890 tower is SPARKPLUG; the story does not describe the shape. 14) McCabe: the Daily Kennebec Journal (21 Feb 1916) and the Manchester Journal (24 Feb 1916) print the keeper's name as Joseph R. McCabe; the archive and the Bulletins give Joseph B. McCabe. The story treats them as one keeper on the strength of the dates and post; the newspapers do not give a middle initial that matches the archive. 15) Inspector William W. Buchanan is named from LighthouseFriends' account of the 1910 report; the Board report itself was not read. 16) Lighthouse Service Bulletin quotations use OCR corrections in the story ('bell' for 'beU'); the evidence entries keep the OCR text.
